A palimpsest is a writing surface reused after an earlier text has been erased or scraped away, while traces of the earlier writing remain. By extension, it describes something whose present form carries marks of earlier forms beneath it.
The image fits a knowledge garden when a page brings an original source together with later commentary: the source remains legible, while annotations add another layer of meaning.

Medieval scribes reused parchment because preparing it was costly. Erasing the surface did not always remove the earlier text completely, leaving the older writing partly legible beneath the new text.
A literal manuscript palimpsest reuses one physical surface. A digital garden can preserve distinct source and commentary pages, then present them together as a layered reading.
A source page can remain the record of what another garden says, while a local discussion page holds interpretation and response.

A Database/View can present the source and commentary together without making either layer stand in for the other. The combined view is palimpsestic in its reading experience, though the underlying digital pages are separate.
Palimpsest · French Ministry of Culture defines the manuscript form as reused parchment where the erased original remains partly readable.

A paradox is a statement or situation that seems self-contradictory or absurd yet is supported by reasoning that looks sound. From the Greek paradoxon, "contrary to expectation."

Veridical — the conclusion sounds absurd but is true. The Monty Hall problem and the birthday paradox, in which 23 people are enough for even odds that two share a birthday, both hold up under calculation.
Falsidical — the conclusion is false because the argument hides a mistake. Zeno's paradoxes of motion fall apart once an infinite sum of shrinking steps is allowed to add up to a finite distance.

Antinomy — accepted reasoning leads to a true contradiction, which forces a change to the assumptions. The liar paradox ("this sentence is false") and Russell's paradox about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves are the classic cases; Russell's led to the axioms of modern set theory.

A paradox marks the spot where an intuition or a theory breaks. Working one out usually means giving up an assumption nobody had noticed they were making, which is why paradoxes have driven changes in logic, mathematics and physics.
Person/Erwin Schrödinger/Cat is a paradox built on purpose, to show where a theory of quantum measurement leads.
Jevon's Paradox — efficiency gains that make a resource cheaper can raise its total use.
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Paradoxes and Contemporary Logic
Having the nature of a Paradox: seemingly contradictory or absurd, yet possibly true or well founded.
In everyday use it also describes behavior or results opposite to what one would expect, as in a drug's paradoxical effect.
Parallax is the apparent shift in an object's position when it is seen from two different places. Near objects shift more than far ones, so the size of the shift tells how far away something is.
By extension, viewing one subject from several positions reveals a dimension that no single view shows.
Hold a finger at arm's length and close each eye in turn: the finger jumps against the background. Move the finger closer and the jump grows.
The brain merges the two slightly different views from the two eyes into a sense of depth, a process called stereopsis.

Astronomy. As the Earth travels around the Sun, a nearby star shifts against more distant stars. Measuring that shift from opposite sides of the orbit gives the star's distance. A parsec is the distance at which the shift is one arcsecond.

Web design. Parallax scrolling scrolls background layers more slowly than foreground layers, so a flat page appears to have depth. Website/Misato Town gets a related effect another way, by tying scroll position to an animation timeline.

Layered media. A recording published in several layers, from raw session to finished piece, lets a listener compare versions of the same moment, as with the layers planned for GitP/A in Week/Review/26/10/11 Sun. A Palimpsest and a Diagram/Cross-Section show their subject in layers in a similar way.
usually used in contrast to Serial execution contexts or Concurren/t execution sessions
